# University of Chicago Summary
The University of Chicago, founded in 1890 and located in Hyde Park, is a leading private research institution recognized for its academic rigor, influential core curriculum, and emphasis on interdisciplinary scholarship. Its undergraduate college offers Bachelor of Arts and Bachelor of Science degrees across 51 majors and 33 minors, implementing a renowned core curriculum that draws on the Socratic method and Great Books program. Graduate studies are organized into four academic divisions and seven professional schools, including highly ranked law and business schools, and the Pritzker School of Medicine and Molecular Engineering. UChicago operates over 140 research centers and institutes, manages national laboratories like Argonne and co-manages Fermilab, and maintains affiliations with organizations such as the Marine Biological Laboratory. The University of Chicago Library system houses six libraries with 11 million volumes, and the campus features Gothic and modern architecture, historic landmarks, and the Logan Center for the Arts.
As of 2024, the university's endowment is valued at $10.1 billion, with total assets at $20.3 billion and an annual budget exceeding $5 billion. Enrollment includes 7,569 undergraduate and 10,968 graduate students; the undergraduate class of 2025 features 53% male and 47% female students, with significant racial and international diversity. Admission is highly selective, with an undergraduate acceptance rate of 4.7%, and the university is need-blind for domestic applicants. UChicago supports extensive student life, hosting over 400 student organizations and a distinctive house system for residential living. The Maroons varsity teams compete in NCAA Division III, and campus traditions include the annual Scavenger Hunt and Latke-Hamantash Debate. UChicago boasts 101 Nobel laureates, numerous nationally recognized scholars, and influential alumni and faculty across academia, government, business, and the arts.
